changes.before: Create reminders(id,reminder_date) as a view that returns the calendar day after each stored event_date. Dates in this fixture are valid YYYY-MM-DD text dates. Use SQLite date functions, not numeric addition on the string.
changes.after: Use the date function to find the next calendar day.

before: SQLite does not have a dedicated date datatype. Applications choose a consistent supported representation.
This fixture uses YYYY-MM-DD text for calendar dates without a time of day.

date accepts supported date text and modifiers.
```sql
SELECT date('2026-04-30', '+1 day');
```
The result is 2026-05-01. The date function handles the month boundary.
Adding the number 1 to a text date is not calendar arithmetic. Use the date function for this contract.
A leap day is a useful boundary test. The day after 2024-02-28 is 2024-02-29.
Calendar dates are not the same as timezone-aware instants. If your app stores moments, choose and document an explicit timezone/UTC policy separately.
This exercise uses fixed supplied dates, not the current clock, so tests remain reproducible.
after: SQLite has no separate date type. An app chooses a consistent way to store dates.
This project stores valid dates as `YYYY-MM-DD` text: year, month, then day. These values have no time of day.

Run this query:
```sql
SELECT date('2026-04-30', '+1 day') AS reminder_date;
```
The date function reads the date and applies the change `'+1 day'`.
The result is `2026-05-01`. April ends after day 30, so the next day starts May.
Adding the number 1 to date text does not apply calendar rules. Use the date function instead.
A leap year has an extra day in February. Calendar calculations must handle that day as well as month and year boundaries.
A calendar date is different from an exact moment. An app that stores moments also needs a clear rule for time zones.
Create `reminders(id, reminder_date)` as a view that adds one calendar day to each event_date. Keep each event ID. Use the supplied dates, not today's clock, and leave the source events unchanged.

before.question: Why is event_date + 1 not a reliable way to find the next day for a text date?
choices: Numeric addition does not apply calendar month/year rules to the text representation.
Every month has exactly thirty days.
SQLite date functions always use today instead of supplied dates.
before.explanation: Calendar arithmetic has boundaries and representation rules. date(value, "+1 day") interprets the supported date text instead of treating it as an ordinary number.

after.question: Why is event_date + 1 unreliable for a date stored as text?
choices: Plain number addition does not follow calendar rules for that text.
SQLite date functions always use today.
after.explanation: The date function reads the date and handles month, year, and leap-day boundaries.
